hints.junior: There's nothing to find and stop — React 18 Strict Mode double-invokes effects in development on purpose, to catch bugs before production does.
hints.mid: Strict Mode mounts, cleans up, and re-mounts every component once in development, running every effect and its cleanup twice — this never happens in production.
hints.staff: The double-invoke rehearses a real scenario React needs to handle: unmounting and remounting a component while reusing its state.

hints.junior: Only one version actually undoes its subscription when the effect cleans up — trace what that means for the subscription count.
hints.mid: The broken version ends the mount→cleanup→mount sequence with two active subscriptions; the fixed version ends with exactly one.
hints.staff: This comparison is static because the failure only shows up across the mount→cleanup→mount sequence, not within a single render.

hints.junior: The bug was never 'runs twice' — it's that the cleanup function doesn't actually undo what the effect set up.
hints.mid: An effect whose cleanup exactly reverses its setup behaves identically whether it runs once or twice — the double-invoke can't expose a bug that isn't there.
hints.staff: Any effect without a complete inverse in its cleanup is a latent production bug already — Strict Mode just needs the right timing to trigger it, dev or not.

hints.junior: Don't reach for a ref-flag that skips the second run — it hides the warning without fixing the bug, which resurfaces the moment a real remount happens.
hints.mid: fetch calls inside effects need the same fix — cancel the in-flight request in cleanup with AbortController, don't let a stale response land late.
hints.staff: Strict Mode's double-invoke never runs in production — treat any warning as a real correctness bug to fix, not a dev-only quirk to route around.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a useEffect that seemed to run twice for no reason — spoiler, it's on purpose, React Strict Mode does this deliberately in development.
sections.mid: In development, Strict Mode intentionally mounts, cleans up, and re-mounts every component once — every effect runs, its cleanup runs, then it runs again. This never happens in production.
sections.staff: Strict Mode's double-invoke is rehearsing a real scenario your effect will eventually hit anyway — a future React feature that unmounts and remounts a component while reusing its state.

sections.junior: The real fix isn't stopping the double run — it's writing a cleanup function that actually undoes whatever the effect set up, so running it twice is perfectly safe.
sections.mid: An effect whose cleanup exactly reverses its setup behaves identically whether it runs once or twice — the double-invoke only exposes bugs in effects that were never safe to run more than once.
sections.staff: This generalizes beyond subscriptions — any effect with a partial cleanup, one that doesn't cancel an in-flight request or unregister every listener it registered, is a latent production bug even if double-invoke never happened.

sections.junior: Compare two versions of the same effect — only one of them has a cleanup function that actually reverses the subscription it created.
sections.mid: The comparison is static, since the actual failure only shows up over the mount, cleanup, mount sequence Strict Mode runs, not within a single render.
sections.staff: Trace what happens to the subscription count under the double-invoke for each version — the broken one ends with two active subscriptions, the fixed one ends with exactly one.

sections.junior: Strict Mode's double-invoke is a diagnostic, not the bug. Fix the missing cleanup, don't silence the warning.
sections.mid: The fix is never stopping it from running twice — it's writing a cleanup function that fully reverses whatever the effect's setup did.
sections.staff: A ref-flag workaround that skips the second invocation only hides the symptom in dev — the same bug resurfaces in production the moment the component genuinely remounts.
